newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Central Asia leaders call for Afghan peace.
newsitem.headline: Central Asia leaders call for Afghan peace.

text.p: The leaders of the former Soviet Central Asian states of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan laid plans on Thursday for a conference on peace in Afghanistan and pledged to strengthen economic ties.

Kyrgyzstan's Askar Akayev, Uzbekistan's Islam Karimov and Kazakhstan's Nursulatan Nazarbayev met in the mountain lakeside resort of Cholpon Ata, 240 km (150 miles) east of the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, to discuss regional security and improve cooperation.

The three republics, covering a territory larger than Western Europe but populated by just 44 million people, have repeatedly voiced fears that a militant, Taleban-type Islam could spill over their borders from the fighting in Afghanistan.
Akayev came out with an initiative earlier this year for a U.N.-sponsored conference in Bishkek on peace in Afghanistan.
Karimov, whose country borders Afghanistan and who is known as a harsh critic of the purist Taleban militia fighting to install rigid Islamic rules there, eagerly backed Akayev's idea.
"All warring sides must give up military means of resolving their problems and this first of all refers to the Taleban," Karimov told a news conference after the summit.
"We would most actively participate in the Bishkek conference...A civil war in one state creates permanent tension in adjoining territories and we are vitally interested to end the Afghan war."
Akayev said Russia, China and the U.N. secretary general backed the idea of holding the conference. The United Nations would take a final decision later this year, he said.

Nazarbayev spoke of a need to increase cooperation within the Central Asian Union which the three recession-hit republics, united by common roots in old Turkic tribes, set up in 1994 to promote their political, economic and cultural ties.
He said one of the ideas generated during the summit was to set up joint consortia covering such areas as power, engineering, communications and extracting and processing natural resorces.
"Kazakhstan is ready to take part in an energy consortium and will open its market for cheap Kyrgyz electricity," he said.
Akayev said foreign investors would be welcome to take part in the consortia.
But little progess was apparently made in bringing to life the inert Central Asian Bank for Cooperation and Development, set up in 1994 to finance joint projects.

Market reforms have been slower in Uzbekistan, whose controversial multiple exchange rate mechanism prevents mutual convertibility of the three states' currencies and the bank lacks the capital to launch big investment projects.
